title: Does an AI reading earnings reports actually add anything over plain momentum?
author: TheObserverDev
selftext:
I’ve been running a paper trading experiment where an AI scores every earnings report (0-100) for stocks that already passed a momentum screen (big 1 and 5 year gains). The bots buy the high scores.

Then I ran a backtest where one bot completely ignored the AI score and just bought whatever went up the most in the past year. Same rules otherwise.

Results were mixed. With 80 stocks, the AI version did a bit better. With 20-30 stocks, the dumb momentum bot did way better, the AI score seemed to filter out some of the biggest winners.

So now I’m running both live side by side until Christmas to see what happens.

For people who’ve tried using LLMs on fundamentals: did you find they add real value, or is the momentum doing all the work? And is there a better way to test this than what I’m doing?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
two things I'd check before reading anything into it.

first, the backtest half. if the model scoring old earnings reports was trained after those dates, it may already know how the stock did next, and the score quietly leaks the outcome. the live run to Christmas is the clean version, the backtest probably isn't.

second, the 20-30 stock result is what you'd expect from momentum alone. most of the gain comes from two or three huge names, so any filter that drops even one of them loses. a better control than the dumb bot is a random filter: drop the same number of stocks at random, a few hundred times, and see where the AI version lands in that spread. if it beats most of the random drops, the score is doing something. if it sits in the middle, the momentum is doing the work and the score is noise.

replies.author: TheObserverDev
replies.body: cloude did the math,  here it is:  great idea on the random filter, I ran it. 500 random drops of the same number of stocks (about a third). the AI filter landed around the 21-28th percentile depending on portfolio size, so worse than the typical random drop but not crazy far out. by your rule thats noise, momentum is doing the work. and you’re right about the backtest, if anything look-ahead should have helped the AI and it still didn’t. so the live race is the real test now

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
respect for actually running it. 21st-28th percentile against random drops is a clean answer, and better to learn momentum is doing the work now than after Christmas.

that random-drop control is something I lean on in Quantradin too, a free thing I built that replays a stock rule on pretend money. quantradin.com

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Running both side by side is the right test, and the "same rules, only the score removed" setup is the clean way to do it. Two things I'd add. First, an LLM may already know how past earnings reports played out, so the backtest dates need to be after its training cutoff, or the score can look better than it really is. Second, a fair comparison is against random picks from the same momentum-screened list with the same number of stocks, since the gap between 20 and 80 stocks could be luck. Since the results flip with portfolio size, I'd treat the live run as the real test. Cymetica's Backtest Labs is one place to run that kind of comparison with fees and out-of-sample data.

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body: Since you have already run the random-drop control, I would now freeze the score prompt/model version and the portfolio construction rules for both forward runs. Publish paired daily returns, turnover and which excluded names explain the gap; that will show whether the difference is stock selection or changing exposure. QATS team here. The useful artefact is a reproducible decision log, not just the Christmas winner. Will you retain the original report, score and timestamp for every accepted and rejected candidate?
